sentences.text: This animal possessed a distinct series of bony plates, known as osteoderms, running down its tail.
These tail osteoderms were drop-shaped, longer than wide, and featured a midline ridge with denticles on their irregular outer margins.
The plates were arranged in a double row along the spine, with each vertebra corresponding to two or three pairs of plates.

The holotype specimen, the basis for the species, was discovered by Georg Kandutsch near Jadersdorf in the Gailtal Alps of Carinthia, Austria. It contains parts of the skull, caudal vertebrae, and an articulated distal tail. The specific name kandutschi honors the discoverer. The fossils come from the Partnach Formation, and the taxon is currently considered valid as a new genus and species.

The preserved skull measures 53 mm, leading to an estimated total body length of up to 65 mm for the juvenile specimen. The lack of fusion in certain vertebrae and skull bones indicates that the holotype specimen was not fully mature.

Carinthiasuchus is classified as a member of the clade Poposauroidea. Phylogenetic analyses place it as a member of the early-diverging clade Poposauroidea within Pseudosuchia. Studies indicate that placing Carinthiasuchus in Poposauroidea is more optimal than linking it to other European crocodylomorphs or rauisuchians.
Carinthiasuchus lived during the Ladinian to Carnian stages of the Triassic period. This animal lived in the Partnach Formation of Carinthia, Austria, from the Ladinian to Early Carnian ages.
